SK6031 readonly does not protect a mutable field's contents

readonly constrains the field and never the object in it, so a non-private array or mutable collection is writable by every caller that can see it.

CategoryDesign
Default severitywarning
ScopeSemantic
Needs a compilationyes
Runs under --load=looseno
Cached per fileyes
Fixno
Language version floor—
Since2.0
SupersedesS3887

Why

public readonly string[] Names stops Names = … and stops nothing else. Every caller can still write Names[0] = "…", and on a List<T> can Clear() it — from another thread, at any time, with no compiler complaint anywhere. What makes this worse than declaring the field without the modifier is the reader: readonly is the keyword C# has for "this does not change", so a reviewer who sees it stops looking for the mutation, and static analysis, code review and the type's own documentation all inherit the mistake. A field that must not be written through is either private with a IReadOnlyList<T> property over it, or typed as something that really is immutable — ImmutableArray<T>, FrozenDictionary<K, V>, ReadOnlyCollection<T>. readonly is neither of those and cannot be made into either by adding a keyword.

Example

Instead of:

public sealed class Palette {
    public static readonly string[] Names = ["red", "green"];

    public readonly List<int> Weights = [1, 2];
}

Write:

public sealed class Palette {
    public static readonly ImmutableArray<string> Names = ["red", "green"];

    public IReadOnlyList<int> Weights => weights;

    readonly List<int> weights = [1, 2];
}

When it does not fire

⚠ The mutable types are an explicit list, and an interface test would have been wrong. The obvious implementation asks whether the field's type implements ICollection<T> — and ImmutableArray<T>, ImmutableList<T> and ReadOnlyCollection<T> all implement IList<T>, explicitly, throwing NotSupportedException from every mutator. That implementation reports the immutable collections this rule's own advice tells somebody to switch to, which is the worst answer available. So the rule matches a named set — arrays, List/Dictionary/HashSet/SortedSet/SortedList/SortedDictionary/Queue/Stack/LinkedList, Collection<T> and ObservableCollection<T>, the four mutable generic interfaces, and the non-generic ArrayList/Hashtable/IList/IDictionary/ICollection — resolved through the semantic model, never by the written name. The cost is a miss on a user-defined mutable type, and that is the right direction for a rule whose whole risk is over-firing.

⚠ Concurrent collections are deliberately absent. public readonly ConcurrentDictionary<string, int> Cache is the correct declaration for a shared cache: the type exists to be written through by many callers at once, so the field being non-reassignable is the whole of what anybody expected readonly to mean there. Reporting it would be reporting a design for working as designed. The same argument does not extend to List<T>, which promises nothing about concurrent writers.

A private field is never reported, however mutable it is. The declaring type owns its own state, and readonly there is a note to the type's own author rather than a promise made to anybody else. internal and private protected are reported: both hand the object to code the declaration cannot see, and "the rest of my assembly" is still somebody else at three in the morning.

A zero-length array is exempt. public static readonly string[] Empty = []; has no element anyone could write, so readonly really is the whole guarantee. The three ways to say it — a [] collection expression, Array.Empty<T>() and new T[0] — are all read out of the initializer, per declarator, so readonly int[] a = [], b; reports b and leaves a alone.

A read-only declared type is silence, and that is a known hole. A field typed IReadOnlyList<T> is not reported even when it holds a List<T> that a caller could cast back to and mutate. The rule reads declarations, and that declaration says read-only; catching the cast is a dataflow question about every holder of the value, which is a different rule in a different band.

An unresolved type is silence. If the field's type binds to an error type the rule says nothing, because "not a mutable collection" and "the compilation could not tell" are the same answer from a naive test and only one of them is a finding. This is why the rule is semantic and does not run under --load=loose.

Only arrays and collections, not mutability in general. A public readonly StringBuilder Log has the same defect and is not reported: widening the rule to every mutable object would need a definition of "mutable" that C# does not have, and the collections are where the mistake is both common and unambiguous.

⚠ No fix. The three repairs — change the field's type, make it private and add a read-only property, or drop readonly and admit the field is mutable — are three different decisions about a public API, and two of them break every caller. Choosing between them is exactly the design judgement the finding is asking somebody to make.
